steps.decision: Salt first, every atom counted; then the water, n × 18.
Add the two. Leaving the water out gives the anhydrous salt's Mr, which is a different substance.

What is left of the Mr is all water of crystallisation.
Divide by 18 to count the waters. Stopping at the mass of water is the step most often left out.

options: Because each water molecule has a relative mass of 18
Because there are 18 atoms in the salt
Because x is always 18 or less
whyMenu.explain: x counts water molecules; the water's total mass divided by one molecule's mass, 18, gives how many there are.

steps.decision: Treat the percentages as masses in 100 g and divide each by its Ar.

steps.working: Divide by the smaller: 17.2 ÷ 6.9 = 2.5, so 1 : 2.5; double: 2 : 5, so C2H5.
steps.decision: A ratio of 2.5 is not whole: double both numbers. Rounding 2.5 to 3 or to 2 is the usual slip.

options: Because an empirical formula must be a whole-number ratio
Because hydrogen always comes in pairs
whyMenu.explain: Atoms come whole, so the ratio must be made whole: 1 : 2.5 is the same ratio as 2 : 5.

options.feedback: 2 × 1 + 16. Every water of crystallisation adds 18 to a hydrate's Mr.
That counts one hydrogen. Water has two: 2 × 1 + 16 = 18.
That doubles the oxygen. Water has one oxygen and two hydrogens: 18.

items.stem: How do you find the number of moles in a mass of a substance?

options.text: divide the mass by the Mr
options.feedback: Moles = mass ÷ Mr. This lesson uses it for the salt and the water.

options.text: multiply the mass by the Mr
options.feedback: That gives a far bigger number. Moles = mass ÷ Mr.

options.text: divide the Mr by the mass
options.feedback: Upside down: the mass goes on top. Moles = mass ÷ Mr.

items.stem: What is the ratio 0.10 : 0.30 in its simplest whole numbers?

options.feedback: Divide both by the smaller, 0.10. Empirical formulae and x are found this way.
Whole numbers, but not the simplest: divide both by 10 to get 1 : 3.
The order matters: 0.10 comes first, so 1 : 3.

options.text: water chemically bonded into the crystal structure
options.feedback: Both halves are marks: chemically bonded, into the crystal structure.

options.text: water a salt has been dissolved in
options.feedback: That is a solution. Water of crystallisation is part of the solid crystal.

options.text: water given off when a crystal melts
options.feedback: Heating drives it off, but the definition is where it is: bonded into the crystal.

items.stem: What does heating to constant mass mean?

options.text: heating and weighing repeatedly until two masses are the same
options.feedback: Both actions, repeated, until the mass stops changing.

options.text: weighing the sample again and again without heating
options.feedback: Reweighing alone changes nothing. Heat, cool and weigh, repeating both.
No time is enough on its own: stop when two masses agree.

items.stem: Which division gives x in a hydrate MX·xH₂O?

options.text: moles of water ÷ moles of anhydrous salt
options.feedback: Waters per salt unit.

options.text: moles of anhydrous salt ÷ moles of water
options.feedback: Upside down: that gives a number less than 1.

options.text: mass of water ÷ mass of anhydrous salt
options.feedback: Masses do not count particles. Use moles.
That is the moles of water. Divide it by the moles of salt to reach x.

options.text: the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound
options.feedback: Simplest, whole-number, ratio: all three words matter.

options.text: the actual number of each atom in a molecule
options.feedback: That is the molecular formula.

options.text: a formula showing how the atoms are joined
options.feedback: That is a structural (displayed) formula.

items.stem: A compound has the empirical formula CH₂ and Mr 56. What is its molecular formula?

options.feedback: 56 ÷ 14 = 4 units of CH₂.
That is the empirical formula. Its Mr is 14, not 56: multiply up.
Each unit brings two hydrogens: multiply both numbers.

SrCl₂·6H₂O → ________ + ________
hints: What is left, and how many waters leave?

commonErrors.feedback: Six waters leave: write 6H₂O.

parts.stem:
3.20 g of sulfur burns to form 6.40 g of an oxide of sulfur. (S = 32; O = 16)
Calculate the moles of sulfur.
Calculate the mass of oxygen that reacted.
hints: The oxide's mass minus the sulfur's.

parts.stem: Calculate the moles of oxygen atoms that reacted.
Hence determine the empirical formula of the oxide.

scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2024 C2 Higher: only some reached the empirical formula, despite carried-forward marks.

hints: The moles of S and O, in the simplest whole-number ratio.

commonErrors.feedback: Use the moles, not the masses: 0.1 mol of S to 0.2 mol of O is 1 : 2, so SO₂.

findTheMistake.stem:
Oisín is asked: 'Calculate the Mr of Na₂CO₃·10H₂O. [1]' (Na = 23; C = 12; O = 16; H = 1)
His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The carbonate ion has three oxygen atoms, not two: Na₂CO₃ is 2 × 23 + 12 + 3 × 16 = 106. His water and his adding are right, so the one slip costs the mark.
findTheMistake.feedback: With the third oxygen the Mr is 106 + 180 = 286. Count every atom of the salt before adding the water.

findTheMistake.stem:
Saoirse is asked to find x in MgSO₄·xH₂O: 4.92 g of the hydrate left 2.40 g at constant mass.
Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: x counts waters per salt unit, so the water's moles go on top: 0.14 ÷ 0.02 = 7. A value below 1 cannot be x, since at least one water is bonded to each unit.
findTheMistake.feedback: Her three moles lines are all right. Only the last division is upside down.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ruairí is asked: 'Describe how to heat a hydrated salt to constant mass. [2]'
His method:
studentWorking: Step 2 = add the hydrated salt and weigh again
Step 3 = heat strongly, cool, then weigh
Step 4 = weigh again until two masses are the same
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Weighing again without heating again changes nothing, so the mass cannot fall any further. Constant mass means repeating the heating and the weighing until two masses agree.
correction: Step 4 = heat, cool and weigh again until two masses are the same
findTheMistake.feedback: Steps 1 to 3 are right. Step 4 must repeat the heating too; the 2023 report found this the most common slip.

prompts.answer: Water chemically bonded into the crystal structure.

prompts.prompt: What do hydrated and anhydrous mean?
prompts.answer: Hydrated: contains water of crystallisation. Anhydrous: without water of crystallisation.

prompts.prompt: How do you find the Mr of a hydrate such as CuSO₄·5H₂O?
What does heating to constant mass involve?
prompts.answer: Heat, cool and weigh, and repeat until two masses are the same.

prompts.prompt: How is x found in a hydrate MX·xH₂O from the masses?
prompts.answer: x = moles of water lost ÷ moles of anhydrous salt.

prompts.prompt: Give the colour changes of copper(II) sulfate, heating it and adding water.
prompts.answer: Heating: blue to white. Adding water to the anhydrous salt: white to blue.
The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.

prompts.prompt: How do you get the molecular formula from an empirical formula?
prompts.answer: Divide the molecule's Mr by the empirical formula's Mr, and multiply the formula by that number.

prompts.prompt: Name the type of reaction that removes water of crystallisation by heating.
How should the apparatus for heating a hydrated salt be drawn?
prompts.answer: As a flat, assembled section with every part labelled; a tripod has three legs.

findings.asked: What water of crystallisation means, two Mr values, x from a hydrate's Mr, the masses from a heating experiment and why it was heated and weighed until two masses agreed.
findings.wentWrong: Few could define water of crystallisation; very few found x, usually from a wrong Mr for the anhydrous salt or by not dividing by 18; few could say why the heating and weighing were repeated.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Worked out the salt's Mr, took it from the total, divided by 18, and said the repeats made sure all the water had gone.
findings.rule: x = (Mr of the hydrate − Mr of the salt) ÷ 18; heat to constant mass to remove all the water.

findings.asked: What hydrated means, how to heat to constant mass, and x from the masses before and after heating.
findings.wentWrong: Few defined hydrated; few described constant mass, most often reweighing without heating again; moles were found well, but very few then reached x.
findings.rule: Heat and weigh, and repeat both; x = moles of water ÷ moles of anhydrous salt.

findings.asked: The term for a solid holding water of crystallisation, an Mr, the name of the reaction that removes the water, the method, and the dehydration equation.
findings.wentWrong: The term and thermal decomposition were not well known, nor were the evaporating dish and constant mass; in the equation the 2 in front of the water was often left out or put in front of the salt.
findings.rule: Hydrated; thermal decomposition; evaporating basin, Bunsen burner, constant mass; keep the number in front of the water.

findings.asked: A two-mark definition of water of crystallisation, the name of the reaction, and an empirical formula from masses.
findings.wentWrong: The definition was not well answered; the moles were found well, but only some reached the empirical formula.
findings.rule: Water chemically bonded into the crystal structure; empirical formula from the simplest whole-number ratio of moles.

findings.asked: The terms in a passage, the Mr of a hydrate, and a labelled diagram of the assembled apparatus for removing the water.
findings.wentWrong: The terms were well known; the Mr often lost an oxygen atom; the diagrams were poor: 3-D, instructions not followed, tripods with four legs and labels missing.
findings.rule: Count every atom before adding the water; draw a flat, assembled, labelled section.

findings.asked: The meaning of water of crystallisation.
findings.wentWrong: It was answered much better than in earlier series but still proved hard for some.
findings.rule: Water chemically bonded into the crystal structure.

findings.asked: The practical: describing hydrated magnesium sulfate, recording masses to 2 decimal places, calculating the masses, and describing the anhydrous salt.
findings.wentWrong: The practical was done well; marks were lost for masses not to 2 decimal places, for subtracting the wrong values, and occasionally for white crystals instead of a white powder.
findings.rule: Record every mass to 2 d.p.; subtract the crucible; anhydrous magnesium sulfate is a white powder.

findings.asked: The mass and moles of water lost from hydrated copper(II) sulfate, two Mr values, and the colour change on heating.
findings.wentWrong: Very few turned the mass of water into moles; the hydrate's Mr was harder than the anhydrous salt's; many colour changes were given wrongly.
findings.rule: Moles of water = mass ÷ 18; heating goes blue to white.

findings.asked: x in CuSO4.xH2O from the masses before and after heating, and the colour of the anhydrous salt.
findings.wentWrong: The moles of the anhydrous salt and x challenged some, though carried-forward marks helped; the colour was well known.
findings.rule: Salt's moles from its own Mr; x = water's moles ÷ salt's moles.

findings.asked: What colour anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns once water reaches it.
findings.wentWrong: Very few knew the anhydrous salt is white; colourless was a common wrong answer, though most knew the hydrated salt is blue.
findings.rule: White to blue: the test for water.

insight.ruleToRemember: Water of crystallisation is water chemically bonded into the crystal structure. A hydrate's Mr is the salt's plus n × 18. Heat, cool and weigh, repeating until two masses agree; then x = moles of water ÷ moles of anhydrous salt. An empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of moles.
insight.aStarSignal: Finding x from only a percentage of mass remaining, and explaining how stopping before constant mass lowers x.
